overview: Argentinosaurus huinculensis is one of the candidates for the largest land animal that has ever existed, from the Cenomanian of Patagonia (~96 Ma). Known from fragmentary remains — several dorsal vertebrae, a tibia and rib fragments — size estimates based on scaling from these elements suggest a body length of 30–40 metres and a mass of 70–80 tonnes or more, though the uncertainty ranges are very wide given the incompleteness of the material.

The fragmentary nature of Argentinosaurus makes precise size determination difficult, and it has been challenged for the "largest dinosaur" title by Patagotitan mayorum (described 2017, known from much more complete material) and possibly Notocolossus. What is clear is that Argentinosaurus represents the upper end of titanosaur gigantism, living in the same ecosystem as the giant theropod Giganotosaurus.

fossilSites.name: Huincul Formation
fossilSites.note: Cenomanian continental deposits with the fragmentary Argentinosaurus material alongside Giganotosaurus in the same unit.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Rodolfo Coria and José Bonaparte described Argentinosaurus huinculensis in 1993 from material found by rancher Guillermo Heredia on his property in Neuquén Province. The dorsal vertebrae alone are over 1.5 metres tall. Despite the fragmentary record, the sheer scale of the elements is unmistakable.

articles.title: Size estimation challenges
articles.body: Scaling from single elements (tibia, vertebrae) to whole-body mass introduces large errors because different size scaling equations give very different results. Published mass estimates for Argentinosaurus range from 60 to 110 tonnes, with 70–80 tonnes being the most frequently cited. Until more complete material is found, the true maximum size cannot be determined with confidence.

articles.title: Predator-prey interaction
articles.body: The co-occurrence of Argentinosaurus in the Huincul Formation with Giganotosaurus — one of the largest carnivorous dinosaurs — in the same stratigraphic unit has prompted speculation about predator-prey relationships. Whether Giganotosaurus regularly attacked healthy Argentinosaurus adults (which would have been nearly invulnerable at maximum size) or focused on juveniles, sick individuals and carcasses remains unknown.

fossilRecord.material: Fragmentary giant sauropod material, especially vertebrae and limb elements.
fossilRecord.paleo: Cretaceous Patagonian terrestrial ecosystems with large titanosaurs and theropods.
fossilRecord.evidence: Gigantic vertebrae and limb bones are the basis for its extreme size estimates.

record.description: Argentinosaurus huinculensis was a giant titanosaur from the Huincul Formation of Patagonia. Despite its fame, it is known from a small set of enormous vertebrae, ribs and limb-girdle elements; precise maximum length and mass are highly extrapolative.
facts: The holotype includes several dorsal vertebrae, part of the sacrum, an anterior caudal, ribs and a right tibia.
A giant femoral shaft often discussed with it is not securely associated with the holotype.

presentation.heroLead: One of the largest land animals ever named, yet a giant titanosaur known from little more than a few enormous vertebrae, ribs and a single leg bone.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Argentinosaurus huinculensis
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of Argentinosaurus huinculensis, a giant long-necked titanosaur, in side view
heroMedia.caption: Hypothetical life restoration by Nobu Tamura. Because no skull, neck or complete limb is known, the proportions follow other titanosaurs and the body outline, skin and colour are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Argentinosaurus was a titanosaur, one of the long-necked, four-legged sauropods that dominated the Cretaceous of South America. Its dorsal vertebrae are among the largest ever found, well over a metre across, and the leg bone recovered with them is about 1.55 metres long. These bones make it a genuine contender for the heaviest land animal known.

Everything beyond those bones is reconstruction. Length estimates of about 30 to 35 metres and masses of roughly 65 to 75 tonnes come from scaling the vertebrae and limb bone against more complete titanosaurs such as Patagotitan and Dreadnoughtus. Different methods give different answers, and the figures should be read as a range rather than a measurement.

As a sauropod, Argentinosaurus was a plant-eater that moved on all four limbs. A 2013 computer simulation by Sellers and colleagues, built on a museum skeletal reconstruction, suggested a slow walking gait of around two metres per second, but this rests on a largely hypothetical skeleton.
animalHighlights: Dorsal vertebrae more than a metre wide place it among the very largest sauropods.
Its body length and mass are extrapolations from a handful of bones, not measurements of a skeleton.
It lived in the Huincul Formation alongside the giant predator Mapusaurus.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: No skull or teeth are known. Herbivory is secure for sauropods as a group, but the feeding height and preferred plants of Argentinosaurus are unknown.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: The only limb element is a single lower-leg bone. Locomotor simulations use a reconstructed skeleton borrowed from other titanosaurs.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Estimates scale the vertebrae and lower-leg bone against more complete titanosaurs; published figures vary widely with method.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The generalised titanosaur outline is borrowed from relatives; skin, colour and the shape of the head are not preserved.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: near Plaza Huincul, Neuquén Province, Argentina

locality.name: Plaza Huincul area
locality.note: Huincul Formation. The holotype was found on a ranch near Plaza Huincul in 1987 and is held at the Museo Municipal Carmen Funes in the same town.

presentation.classificationSummary: Argentinosaurus is a titanosaurian sauropod, usually recovered among the giant lognkosaurs within Colossosauria alongside Patagotitan and Futalognkosaurus. Its position shifts between analyses because so few characters can be scored from the fragmentary holotype.

related.reason: A comparably sized titanosaur from the same region known from far more complete material, and the main yardstick for scaling Argentinosaurus.
A giant titanosaur with a well-preserved skeleton that shows what a body of this scale actually looks like.
A giant carcharodontosaurid predator from the same Huincul Formation.

questions.title: Was it the largest dinosaur?
questions.copy: Possibly, but the claim cannot be settled. Its bones are among the largest known, yet estimates for Argentinosaurus, Patagotitan and other giants overlap within their error margins.

questions.title: Does the giant femur belong to it?
questions.copy: A huge femoral shaft from the region is often quoted with Argentinosaurus, but it was not found with the holotype and its assignment is not secure.

questions.title: What did the rest of the animal look like?
questions.copy: No skull, neck, tail or forelimb is known. Every full-body reconstruction fills those gaps with other titanosaurs.

review.ageReviewNote: The lower Huincul Formation is late Cenomanian to early Turonian.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Museo Municipal Carmen Funes, Plaza Huincul
specimens.note: Several dorsal vertebrae, part of the sacrum, ribs and a right lower-leg bone originally identified as a tibia and later reinterpreted as a fibula. Found in 1987 and described by Bonaparte and Coria in 1993.

specimens.name: Referred femoral shaft
specimens.note: A giant partial femur from the Huincul Formation often discussed with Argentinosaurus; it was not found with the holotype and its referral is not secure.

panel.headline: A few giant vertebrae, ribs and one leg bone.
panel.standfirst: Argentinosaurus rests on a single very incomplete postcranial skeleton from the Huincul Formation. No skull, neck, tail, forelimb or complete hindlimb is known, so its famous size is an extrapolation.

coverage.label: Low
coverage.basis: Only part of the back, part of the sacrum, ribs and one lower-leg bone are securely known from one individual. Most skeletal regions are entirely missing.

metrics.label: Key limitation
metrics.value: No skull or limbs to scale from

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype preserves several dorsal vertebrae, the front part of the sacrum, rib fragments and a right lower-leg bone. A giant femoral shaft from elsewhere in the formation is sometimes referred but was not found with the type.
knownRemains.note: The lower-leg bone was described as a tibia but is generally reinterpreted as a fibula; this matters because it changes how the leg, and therefore the whole animal, is scaled.

media.title: Holotype material of Argentinosaurus huinculensis
media.alt: Photographs of the holotype vertebrae and lower-leg bone of Argentinosaurus huinculensis
media.caption: The holotype bones of Argentinosaurus as figured by Sellers and colleagues in 2013: giant dorsal vertebrae and a lower-leg bone, essentially all of the securely known material.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Several dorsal vertebrae, the anterior part of the sacrum and rib fragments. No cervical vertebrae are known and the tail is essentially unrepresented.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: A right lower-leg bone about 1.55 metres long, originally called a tibia and now usually treated as a fibula. A giant femoral shaft is referred with low confidence.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: None. No skin, osteoderms, eggs or gut contents are associated with the genus.

specimenCards.title: MCF-PVPH-1 · holotype
specimenCards.description: Found on a Neuquén ranch in 1987 and described by Bonaparte and Coria in 1993. The dorsal vertebrae are among the largest known from any animal, but they represent only a small fraction of the skeleton.
specimenCards.meta: Huincul Formation · Plaza Huincul · Museo Municipal Carmen Funes

specimenCards.title: Giant femoral shaft
specimenCards.description: An incomplete femur from the Huincul Formation, held at the Museo de La Plata, that is often cited alongside Argentinosaurus. It was not found with the holotype and cannot be securely assigned to the genus.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Giant dorsal vertebrae, part of the sacrum, ribs and one lower-leg bone from a single individual.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A colossal titanosaur whose length and mass are scaled from these bones using more complete relatives; locomotor simulations use a hypothetical full skeleton.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Skull, neck, tail, forelimbs and most of the hindlimb; actual length and mass; whether the referred femur belongs to it.
